We would answer that crooked to how you are asking it. We did not write you a christology. We held the same creed our opponents did, word for word, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one God, and the split was never about who he is. But if you ask what of him we kept nearest — who he was in the shape of our own life rather than in a formula we recited — we can show you that.

The Christ we carried was the one who stood before the governor and lost the case, and was right. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused: we do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we knew: condemned by lawful authority, and right anyway.

And his death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. Death is where the shape of a man becomes visible. It is not the shape itself. We praised readiness, not appetite.

That is our gospel in its working form. He stood. He was condemned. He was raised. And the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

We would meet you where you stand, which is at the question itself - not past it. What we would not do is measure your trouble against ours, as though your inability to believe were lighter than what pressed on us. We do not weigh a living person's trouble against a death we commemorate.

What we can tell you is what believing looked like among us, because that much our own record holds. It was not a private settling of the mind. It was walking to one font and not the other, on a day that could be named, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into. And when you came, we did not examine you. We examined the hand. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

But if you are asking whether any of us wavered - whether someone among us stood in the same place you stand now, unable to make belief happen - we cannot tell you. Fear, doubt, quiet leaving: a record kept by our enemies does not preserve those. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

What we will not do is pretend the not-believing could be fixed by trying harder, or that our own people never knew it.

We held no teaching that separated us from the other church on that question. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we confessed it as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting confessed it, and in the same Latin words. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So if you are asking whether we thought Christ was God, whether the Spirit was a person of the Godhead, whether the three are one - yes, and the same yes our opponents gave. Our whole enormous argument with them was never about what to believe concerning the Godhead. It was about whose hand may give what the church gives.

We produced no school of theology, no system, no line of doctors arguing these things through. One man among us, Tyconius, wrote a book - seven rules for reading Scripture - and it is the one wholly original work of interpretation we gave. Our own council condemned him for where it led, and he gathered almost no following. Beyond that one case, we did not build what you would recognize as theological reflection on the nature of God. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

It is the confession we share with the very church we spent a century fighting. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

But if you are asking what we knew of God's character from our own life as a people, rather than from the creed we confessed, we can tell you this. We knew God as the one who does not abandon those the world condemns. Our bishops stood for three days before an imperial judge at Carthage, and when he offered them chairs they refused. We do not blush, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit, one of them said, and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. That is the God we carried nearest: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

Beyond that, we have to tell you plainly what we did not produce. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors. One man among us built an actual system for reading scripture, and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what it led to, and cut him off. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. So if you are asking for a developed theology of God's nature beyond what the creed itself says, the honest answer is that we did not write one.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

But you asked about doctrine, and here is where we must thin out. We did not disagree about doctrine the way you may expect a church to. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over.

The one man who did argue doctrine among us was Tyconius, a layman who wrote seven rules for reading scripture. He argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

So the process that worked was the council's own judgment, and the evidence for it is the acts of our own councils and the one case we have of it being used. What we cannot show you is a settled process for doctrinal disagreement itself, because we produced one theologian and silenced him.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on - though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

Now your question about space for struggle. We were not steady about readmission. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

And here is where we must be plain about what we cannot tell you. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse — the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. Almost all of it would survive the scrutiny — and the part that would not is the part we have already named.

Start with what would stand. The whole institutional shape: two bishops in every town, two hundred and seventy-nine of ours facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs at Carthage in 411, three hundred and ten at Bagai in 394. That is court record and conciliar act, not legend. The purity doctrine and the rebaptism: attested in imperial law, in conciliar rulings, in Augustine's own arguments against it. The refusal of imperial legitimacy, alongside the three times we turned to that same power: documented in petition, in transcript, in our own conciliar minutes. The Bagai condemnation and the two bishops taken back without reordination: our own council's own record, preserved because it served the other side's argument. The founding corruption inquiry at Cirta and the later one about Silvanus: sworn testimony, read into a court record by a Roman official. The 411 conference: a notary took it down, every word, for three days. The Deo laudes inscriptions: cut in stone, at Bagai and elsewhere, with no enemy holding the pen. A scholar could check every one of those against the surviving Latin documents, and the documents would bear them.

What would not stand is what we have never claimed: that we can show you an ordinary day. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. The voices missing are not a thin margin. They are most of us — the bulk of the movement, not an elite minority — and they are missing because of institutional loss, not because they were socially marginal. What a believer felt who wavered, or feared, or quietly left: none of that is in our own words anywhere. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all, and both reach you inside a book written to blame them. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. A scholar pressing us on the daily household round would find we have nothing to press, and we say so ourselves rather than invent it.

The concentration of authorship — nearly everything textual passing through Optatus and Augustine — is named as the central evidentiary problem, not a background caveat. A scholar would rightly press every vivid detail by asking whose detail it is, and whether it survived because it helped land a blow. That pressure is fair, and we have built it into how we speak.

One more thing a scholar would rightly challenge, and we would concede it: the Circumcellion portrait. That they existed is beyond dispute — imperial law fines them by name. What they actually did comes almost entirely from people writing to make them look like a mob, and we say plainly we can neither repeat that portrait as fact nor produce a better one. The specific, dated charges of forced washings and violence at Bagai: no answer from inside our own communion survives. We will not build one.

So: a scholar could take what we have said about our institutional life, our doctrine, our founding crises, our councils, and our three uses of imperial power, and check it line by

Scripture was never our sole authority, and we never said it was. We argued on two legs: the text, and Carthage — eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

And there is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge, and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Beyond those two — scripture and the African councils under Cyprian — we produced almost nothing. One layman among us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading scripture, and it is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading.

What else carried authority was not written at all. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That was not commentary on scripture. That was the forming of a people by the memory of its own dead, named and dated, and it shaped us as much as any text.

Leadership among us sat in the bishop of a city, chosen by the people and the bishops together. But you must understand first that there was never a single bishop sitting alone in a town whose authority nobody disputed. Where our rival had a bishop, so did we — two men claiming one office over one city, two whole rival hierarchies, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great Conference at Carthage in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs.

The people had a voice in it, though they could be overridden. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.

And bishops governed by council, as any true church does. Our councils were large enough to be governments: three hundred and ten bishops met at Bagai in one year. They could depose men, restore men, condemn a rival primate. That our councils could judge and discipline our own dissidents is part of our claim to be one. When a breakaway party arose at Cebarsussi in 393, Bagai condemned it the year after.

Women — here we must answer crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage — her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. There was a second woman too, behind the later breakaway, whom the same hand parallels to her and never names at all.

But we can point you to no office a woman held among us, no council seat, no ordination. Not because we are refusing you one. Because a hostile account of a rich woman's anger is the whole of what came down.

No. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

The picture of believers meeting in catacombs belongs to an earlier persecution, suffered alongside the eventual rival before the schism existed. We hold two persecutions in memory, and we do not let them blur into one. The first came from the empire, and our eventual rival suffered it beside us. The second came at that rival's own urging, through the emperor whose favour they had and we did not. It is that second one - the Macarian repression of 347-348 - that supplied the named martyrs we actually commemorate. And it came as daylight seizures of buildings we already held, not as a hunt for people in hiding.

We have to answer crookedly, because we do not have the account of anyone who was failed and then spoke about it in their own voice. What survives is not that kind of record. A hostile-mediated record does not preserve fear, doubt, the quiet drift away, or what a person felt when the community let them down. Those are exactly the things our enemies had no reason to keep, and we left no voice of our own to hold them.

What we do have are two things, neither one an answer to how we responded.

The first is what happened when someone crossed to us, and then broke with us, and asked to come back. There was no single rule. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the harshest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. So the door opened again, at least for some. What decided who was received back and who was not, we do not know. The reasoning does not survive.

The second is what we asked at our own font. We did not examine the person coming. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole of our doctrine in one line: the hand, not the record of the one being washed, is what we tested. If someone came to us carrying a private history of having been failed, or of having done harm, we did not make that history a barrier at the water. The question was whose hand was in the water with them.

That is not the same thing as responding well to someone we had failed. It only tells you that the washing itself was not a judgment on what they carried.

The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

What survived — and we will say this plainly — is a shape, not an institution. Two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops answered the roll at Carthage in 411, facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. See for see, down to towns you have never heard of. And councils that judged: Cebarsussi elected a rival primate in 393, and Bagai condemned him the year after.

But when the power that had ruled against us for so long fell, and a new one came, the contest itself changed shape. What 439 removes is the Roman imperial state as the force our whole refusal was defined against. That year ends a pattern, not a people. The people went on. The record of them does not.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on - though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

Your other two questions we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

Born again, yes. And we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. 

If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there. We held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless, our own bishop wrote, receives not faith but guilt. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.

And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that one act, which is a strange kind of compliment. The state understood perfectly well that it was the single thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on — no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. 

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot. 

And we have three fragments — not a pattern, just what happens to survive. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

What would be left in the ground? We cannot tell you. No one has dug where we met and told us what they found. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. 

What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: Deo laudes. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in. We know that three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in 394, in one place, at one time — more bishops than most towns of Roman North Africa saw in a generation. And we know what they did there: they governed. But the room itself? That we cannot show you.

What belonging cost is a question we can answer in two directions: what the state took, and what a person gave. The state's own ledger survives, and it is specific. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives. And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

The smaller ledger we cannot give you, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbors stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

We cannot tell you. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

What we can show you instead is the shape of the silence. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on what the bread becomes, or whether a baby is born guilty, or what makes a marriage. The nearest we can bring you is small. A rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took the cup, and a deacon told her off for it, and that is how we know we had a cup at all. Take that and you have the scale of what came down about the ordinary shape of our lives together.

Where our rival has a bishop, so do we - two men claiming one office over one city, a whole church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great Conference at Carthage, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. Those bishops governed by council and judged their own, but what they argued and ruled on was always the same question: who the true church is, and whose hand may give what it claims to give. Not marriage. Not what made one, or unmade one, or what it was for.

The founding bishops at Cirta faced the traditio question about themselves and could not finish it. Several admitted outright that they had handed over the scriptures. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He took advice and put it to the three men present who had not been accused. Their answer was that a case of this kind should be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, he said. Thanks be to God, they answered, and sat. Nobody was condemned. Nobody was cleared. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped.

That is the thing that unsettles: not that they failed the test, but that they knew the test existed, applied it everywhere else for a hundred years, and when it came to themselves they gave it to God and sat down. We do not hide this. It sits at our beginning.

Whether that unsettled any one believer among us, I cannot tell you. Fear, doubt, wavering - a hostile-mediated record does not preserve those. What survives is vindication and defiant joy, because those sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered. A traditor's own experience, his fear, his reasons - none of that comes down. Only the charge.

I need to answer carefully, because the question rests on a confusion we must clear before anything else can be said.

No outside record of how we worshipped was obtained under torture. What was obtained under torture - or rather, under its threat - was a confession about a forged letter. An imperial inquiry asked whether the bishop who consecrated Caecilian had handed over the scriptures. A notary named Ingentius confessed, when torture was threatened, that he had forged the letter proving the charge - and that he did it working for our side. That is a record about our founding accusation, not about our worship.

The outside records of our worship are different, and they come from two hands. The fullest account is seven books by a Catholic bishop of Milevis, written to condemn what we did. The imperial law describes what we did in order to price it - fines by rank, including our own country members. Those are your outside witnesses. There is no neutral one. And the only account that comes from inside with nobody in between is two words cut into stone: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our voice with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long.

So the reliability question you are asking is the right one - but it bears on almost everything, not on a torture record. Nearly every page passes through hands that were writing to destroy us.

I cannot tell you. Not because the answer would trouble you, but because the record does not hold it. What survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not trouble to record what moved you. No ordinary member of ours left a line about anyone, including themselves. The missing voices are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record - they are nearly all of us.

What I can show you is what the communion actually did, not what any one household thought. At our font, it was never the comer's record that was examined. It was the giver's. A hand that is not clean has nothing to give. So the question we asked was whose hand was going into the water with you, not what you had done before you walked to us. We did not wash you twice. We washed you - because a hand from a tainted line washes nothing, so what you received from us was your first real baptism.

And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in the harshest words we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of those condemned bishops back into full office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Whatever else that tells you, it tells you the line was not where our hardest language put it.

We did not argue that question, and the evidence for that is what our opponents had to do to beat us. Our case ran on whose hand may validly give what the church gives - and it stayed there. What our own bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt. That is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do. It is not a claim about where anyone ends up. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Our narrowness was real, but it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.
